title: Shadow-to-solo oncall progression and 24h micro-postmortem toolkit
author: Maya R. Chen
body:
Overview

This page documents a lightweight, operationally focused path for new responders to progress from shadowing an oncall to handling incidents solo, plus a standardized 24-hour micro-postmortem template and customer-facing status message patterns. The intent is to reduce time-to-autonomy while preserving incident evidence fidelity and consistent customer communication.

Goals
- Reduce mean time to autonomous oncall from 12 weeks to 6 weeks via staged competency gates.
- Ensure every incident has actionable, timebound next steps in the first 24 hours.
- Provide ready-to-use status-page and CSR templates for rapid customer notification.

Scope
Applies to: SREs, runtime engineers, platform oncall rotation members, responder apprentices. Not intended for long-form postmortems (these continue to use the existing postmortem rubric). This is a rapid follow-up and training scaffold for incidents that:
1) affect customer-facing latency or availability, or
2) trigger rollback or capacity action.

Ownership and success metrics
- Owner: Oncall Enablement (engineering).
- Success metrics: fraction of new responders fully approved after staged progression, average time from incident closure to 24h micro-postmortem completion (target < 36 hours), completeness score on evidence checklist (target 95%).

Roles and responsibilities
- Primary responder (PR): performs triage, containment, and documents timeline.
- Shadow (S): follows PR, asks clarifying questions, performs guided tasks.
- Mentor/approver (M): validates competencies and approves stage progression.
- Bridge operator (BO): coordinates cross-team activities and status updates if incident escalates.

Staged progression: Shadow -> Guided -> Lead with Mentor -> Solo with Mentor Review -> Solo
Each stage has a checklist. Progression is gated: Mentor signs off in the internal training tracker. Typical cadence: 2–3 incidents per stage or 2 weeks of rotations, whichever comes first.

Stage 0 — Observational shadow (Days 0–7)
- Objective: learn the monitoring, runbooks, and pager flow.
- Checklist:
  1) Observe 5 incoming alerts and confirm understanding of alert signal and SLO impact.
  2) Watch a full bridge/incident flow once (10–30 min).
  3) Show the mentor where runbooks live and how to find the top-3 telemetry panels.
  4) Run through the status page UI and demo sending a private-stage update (no public send).

Stage 1 — Guided actions (Weeks 1–2)
- Objective: complete non-timecritical remediation tasks with a mentor.
- Checklist:
  1) Execute containment steps from a non-privileged runbook with mentor guidance (sample: scale down noisy pod, apply rate limit).
  2) Collect evidence artifacts listed in "Incident evidence checklist" below.
  3) Draft a customer status note and have mentor review.

Stage 2 — Lead with mentor (Weeks 3–5)
- Objective: lead triage and containment in low-to-medium severity incidents; mentor approves actions.
- Checklist:
  1) Own the incident bridge for a low-sev incident under mentor observation.
  2) Perform rollback / capacity steps if required and document commands exactly.
  3) Produce the 24h micro-postmortem and assign next steps.

Stage 3 — Solo with post-incident review (Weeks 6–8)
- Objective: handle single-team incidents solo; mentor reviews post-incident writeup within 48 hours.
- Checklist:
  1) Clear ownership on bridge, run responder playbook end-to-end.
  2) Create customer-facing status updates as needed.
  3) Complete 24h micro-postmortem and evidence collection.

Stage 4 — Full solo (graduation)
- Objective: autonomous responder across sev1–2 incidents with periodic mentor calibration.
- Checklist:
  1) Mentor signs off after reviewing 3 solo incidents and passing the competency quiz.
  2) Added to rotation as full responder.

Competency gates and assessment
- Practical: have the candidate run through a simulated incident (game day mini-lab) and execute containment steps in a sandbox.
- Knowledge: 20-question quiz covering runbooks, SLOs, and comms templates (pass threshold 80%).
- Evidence: confirmed evidence artifacts for 3 incidents.

Incident evidence checklist (minimum required for 24h follow-up)
- Timestamped timeline (ISO 8601).
- Triggering alert details: alert name, KPI that tripped, threshold value.
- Command log: exact CLI/API commands executed (copy/paste).
- Relevant logs/snippets (log id + 100-line context or link to log view).
- Top-level telemetry screenshots or dashboard links (p95, p99, error rate, throughput).
- List of attached runbooks and sections used.
- Owner and stakeholders contacted (bridge, oncall, product manager, CSR).
- Short summary (1–3 sentences) and proposed remedial action(s).

24-hour micro-postmortem template
Use this minimal, actionable postmortem for incidents that require a fast, evidence-backed follow-up. Complete within 24 hours; send to mentor and stakeholders. If the incident meets the long-postmortem criteria, convert to full postmortem.

- Title: [Service] — short description (sev, region)
- Incident start / end: ISO timestamps
- Severity classification: SEV1|SEV2|SEV3
- Impact summary: bullet list of user-visible effects and approx. affected customers
- Timeline (ordered bullets): timestamps + one-line events
- Root cause hypothesis: short paragraph
- Immediate mitigations taken: bullet list with exact commands/actions
- Evidence bucket: list of evidence artifacts (logs, dashboards, recordings) with links
- Customer comms sent: paste status-page message(s) and delivery timestamps
- Action items (owner, due date, priority): 1–5 items, timeboxed to < 30 days
- Decision: escalate to long form postmortem? yes/no (criteria: data loss, regulatory impact, repeated regression)

Game-day mini-labs (designed for progression and assessment)
- Lab 1 — Alert Triage and Evidence Capture (30–45m): receive simulated alert, find dashboard panels, collect evidence, draft 24h micro-postmortem.
- Lab 2 — Throttle and Cache Eviction Scenario (45–60m): simulate a sudden KV cache eviction across a single region; practice rollback and cross-region traffic shift.
- Lab 3 — Status Page and CSR Messaging (30m): craft multistage status updates for a progressively improving incident; include escalation paths and templates.

Scoring rubric for labs (pass/fail plus qualitative notes)
- Evidence completeness (0–5): were all mandatory artifacts captured?
- Communication clarity (0–5): was the status message concise and accurate?
- Command accuracy (0–5): were the remediation steps safe and reversible?
- Time to containment (observational): recorded by mentor.

Status page and customer message templates
- Short public update (initial): "We are investigating increased request latency for the Redwood Inference hosted API in us-west-2. Our team is actively triaging. Users may experience higher-than-normal response times. Next update: in 30 minutes or when we have an actionable update."
- Update when mitigations active: "We have routed traffic away from the impacted capacity pool and applied a temporary throttle. Error rate reduced from 8% to 1.2%. We continue to monitor and will provide a more detailed follow-up within 4 hours."
- Customer-facing resolution: "Service performance has been restored to expected levels. Root cause analysis is in progress and a 24-hour follow-up will be posted once evidence capture is complete. If you were affected, please open a support ticket and include your request IDs so we can prioritize."
- CSR private lane snippet (for billing/credits): "Affected customers may be eligible for a service credit. Please collect tenant_id, start/end times, and request_ids. Escalate to Support Lead for approval."

Runbook patterns (practical guidance)
- Always run in a copy/paste-friendly shell: paste commands into incident notes.
- Prefer non-destructive containment first (traffic reroute, scaling, circuit breakers) before stateful rollbacks.
- When running a rollback: note the exact image/tag and cluster + node IDs, and include a post-rollback verification checklist.

Runbook retirement and remedial task tracking
- Remedial tasks created during micro-postmortem must be triaged into the backlog within 72 hours.
- For long-lived fixes (>2 weeks): create a tracked ticket with a remediation owner and quarterly review.
- Runbooks updated post-incident must include a changelog entry with author and date.

Appendix: quick commands and links
- Useful commands (examples):
  - kubectl -n redwood logs deploy/runtime --since=30m | sed -n '1,200p'
  - kubectl -n redwood rollout undo deploy/runtime --to-revision=42
  - curl -sS 'https://api.redwood-infra/internal/health' | jq '.'
- Important internal links:
  - Oncall rotation roster: [link to roster in HR wiki]
  - Central runbook index: [link to runbook index]
  - Incident evidence S3 bucket: s3://redwood-incident-evidence/<incident-id>/

Appendix B: when to convert to a full postmortem
Convert if any of the following are true:
- Customer data loss or regulatory exposure
- Incident lasted > 4 hours for a SEV1 or > 12 hours for SEV2
- Material billing/crediting impact or repeated regressions in the last 90 days

Change log
- 2025-05-20: Initial draft and staged progression added (Maya R. Chen).
- 2026-10-12: Added lab scenarios and updated evidence checklist based on SRE retro (Aisha Patel).

Notes & references
- This document is intended to complement existing incident lifecycle and postmortem standards. See the central incident rubric for full postmortem guidance and evidence retention policies.
